content:
This thread is intended to revive discussion on algorithmic frameworks : cslib#372 (renewed at cslib#685) and cslib#401 .

Per recent discussion in cslib#401 github comments, this PR is being discussed in the reviewer channels on this Zulip. However since I cannot know or contribute to the discussion there, I am starting this thread.

  1. As of today morning it is fairly clear, even by the half-correct PR description of cslib#401 that it is a cosmetic change over cslib#372 (the main false claim being that any of the reviews of 401 contributed in any way to cslib#372 in the first place, other than making it a closer copy, since cslib#372 acquired everything including the lower bound before cslib#401).
  2. From a pure OSS contribution norms and ethics perspective this makes cslib#401 a duplicate PR of cslib#372. In any other scenario a duplicate PR would be marked as such and closed. An ethical contributor would not rebuild an existing PR or make spurious claims of superiority as has been the case here in prior threads, when the work essentially duplicates the existing PR. They would make a PR with their proposed improvements to the existing PR or offer reviews. Neither of these things has happened.
  3. In the meantime, leaving these ethical issues aside (which already ought to be the deciding argument), as far back as early June 2026, in the weekly CSLib online meetings, it was agreed there there would be a video call discussion on the algorithms PRs. To this end I extended an olive branch by including cslib#401's history into cslib#372. It was intended to acknowledge the fact that by independently starting on a different idea and converging to cslib#372, the PR cslib#401 established the robustness of cslib#372. The result was cslib#685. It has since been extended by @Samuel Schlesinger's improvement of the lower bound proof.
  4. The meeting itself has not so far. Yet a reviewer is already talking of merging a technically inadequate PR cslib#401.

All of this as far as I am concerned, amounts to a complete disregard of basic contribution ethics for the convenience of an AI-powered senior contributor, whose PR offers no meaningful improvement after 6 months. Note, I am more than willing to accept the sparse cosmetic improvements into cslib#685. In the meantime, a substantial body of work has accumulated downstream of the work of cslib#372/cslib#685, on

  • upper bounds,
  • lower bounds,
  • query composition and reduction composition,
  • randomised algorithms,
  • mvcgen integration,
  • circuits, and
  • quantum algorithms,

much of which would meaningfully fit into CSLib. I hope we can move forward with cslib#685 which duly includes everyone in the git credit history.

I am also willing to propose specific elements of cslib#401 which can be PRed to cslib#685 and equally, accept further reviews and refinements of cslib#685 as long as the integrity of the basic design is not affected.

Merging cslib#401 offers no benefits over cslib#685, but

  1. Negates my work for no justifiable reason (I handwrote most of the code, only the lower bound was AI written for time reasons, and this after I gave specific instructions).
  2. Makes subtoptimal choices for models.
  3. Makes upstreaming existing content pointlessly tedious. In fact without bundled models, it makes the content of model composition and reduction convoluted.
CC : @Tanner Duve , @Fabrizio Montesi , @Alexandre Rademaker , @Eric Wieser

In fact without bundled models, it makes the content of model composition and reduction convoluted.

Can you elaborate on the purpose of bundled models in your PR description? Right now the only justification given there is

We bundle costs and models together since these together define a computational model and we can speak of reductions between models using Progs.

This to me looks like the main technical difference between the PRs. I don't think it makes sense to discuss here without an initial pitch for the benefit of that part of design.

1. There’s the conceptual point. A model is by definition a combination of its unit operations and their costs. For example variants of RAM such as integer vs word ram and custom arithmetic models based on them. They support the same operations which evaluate the same way but differ in costs.
  2. I am not allowed to discuss the downstream code repo on this channel which explains how it is used. But it is highly relevant. Roughly. A query type can represent the ADTs of data structures. When you want to formalise an algorithm which uses many data structures, the straightforward way is to build a query model which is the direct sum of these data structure ADT query types. We can construct the composite models of these types from their individual models.
  3. extending the above: we can compositionally define the reduction of two query types and their models to a common model. So if you have a stack ADT and a queue ADT and their reductions to RAM, you can compose these reductions.

all the code of 2 and 3 is pointlessly duplicated if you split the model. Some code for this already exists in Algolean

Also 401, defines a query count for some mysterious reason. The only use is in lower bounds. However lower bounds can be more general and cost based. Further the query counts are just a special case for cost.

Note that the query complexity model is a way to formalize algorithms theory top down. Reductions are how we justify such an approach. So you can justify using “literature oracles” to formalize some recent STOC paper on the assumption that once the literature algorithm authors formalize algorithms for those oracles they immediately give you an algorithm in a lower level model. Eventually we hope to get to basic machine models. Reductions are the mechanism to do this. Thus they need to be supported well. Each literature oracle might have different cost functions depending on which paper it is derived from and therefore require a separate reduction, whether or not they have the same eval function. We need to support both cases uniformly.
@Eric Wieser any further comments?

I have edited the PR description of cslib#685 to explain bundling.

I had a look at the new attempt to write algorithms with a monad polymorphic style only to specialize it to FreeM in cslib#401 just now.

  1. For algorithms theory this is a meaningless change. One could write all monadic code like this (including Lean's metaprogramming monad hierarchy). This is just one way of writing MTL-style transformers. That doesn't mean it adds anything meaningful here if you only ever want to use FreeM for algorithmic analysis.
  2. It doesn't scale well to large query types where each of the operations may be used. Comparison sort hides scalability issues like this by using only one query. A graph algorithm using stacks, queues, and priority heaps will needlessly add 8-10 parameters for each operation just to lower it into a free monad of a composite of three pre-defined and reusable query types.

CC : @Eric Wieser since you requested the PR description change and I only just saw the edit
Let’s move this message to #computer science first please. This is a bit off topic

@Sebastian Zimmer alternatively if you could rewrite this message in another topic in #computer science and delete this message here, we can continue the discussion on that thread. This thread is for comparing the two PRs only.

A summary of the situation, since messages are scattered all over the place:

  • @Alexandre Rademaker has been working to set up a meeting, but some of the relevant people were doubtful that it would lead to a resolution given how several previous interactions had gone. I can understand that. Concerns raised about the conduct of other contributors have already been reviewed through the appropriate CoC and Zulip moderation channels; the CoC subsequently posted a public message supportive of those contributors. Anyone who wants to pursue conduct or moderation aspects further is welcome to contact the CoC or Zulip moderation teams. I don't think relitigating those issues here is going to help resolve the situation.

  • Public discussion and direct communication have proven ineffective, and there has been substantive disagreement about some of the technical claims made in this and other threads. I've therefore asked the wider CSLib reviewer/maintainer group to (i) review the open PRs and surrounding discussion, and (ii) form a joint proposal for how to bring this to a conclusion, both technically and regarding attribution. Any concrete information or evidence posted here will of course be taken into account as part of that review.

To add to the above I submitted a proposal to Fabrizio that combines the two PRs in a technically beneficial way that also ensures that unethical conduct with PR duplication and scooping is not rewarded. Quoted below

I have a proposal that includes both PRs. It goes into some detail. But it both optimizes the design + implementation, and it minimises maintenance and upstreaming overheads.

Briefly:

  1. Merge cslib#685 (everyone is attributed). Models are bundled so we can build the reduction graph.
  2. Make a PR to add cslib#401's mergeSort with minor adaptations to the bundled models
  3. Upstream algolean algorithms (including basic named algorithms) and mvcgen integration.

There are still some technical drawbacks in cslib#401's implementation.
(And I did forward that to the working group, as promised.)

In order to make a stronger case for bundling of models I thought I might share this file from algolean which states general notions of uniform correctness and transporting correctness notions over reductions. These theorems will look substantially worse without model bundling as is the case in cslib#401.

CC : @Alexandre Rademaker since you are reviewing these PRs.

Additional Notes : There is now a basic WordRAM model built on top of cslib#685. It relies on a generalisation of models called ModelM that our PRs downstream version has. There are also two variants of randomised quicksort.

Update : We have a foolproof deep embedding of WordRAM algorithms in the query-combinator model of cslib#685. The idea of cross-posting this here came up in the online meeting today. This relies on bundling evaluation and cost even more tightly :
#CSLib > WordRAM design proposal for CSLib @ 💬

Given that, per above, the only differentiation between cslib#685 and csli#401 is model bundling, I would say merging cslib#685 and upstreaming this piecemeal is the cleanest path forward.
